newsitem.title: USA: Jackson defends Oakland in black English dispute.
newsitem.headline: Jackson defends Oakland in black English dispute.

text.p: Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson on Monday defended Oakland's educators who have come under fire over a controversial plan to recognise black English in the classroom.

Jackson, who initially criticised the school board's proposal as "an unacceptable surrender borderlining on disgrace," met with Oakland school officials and advisers to be briefed on the district's plans. Afterwards, Jackson said Oakland's board had been misunderstood.
"They're not trying to teach black English as a standard language. They're looking for tools to teach children standard English so they might be competitive," Jackson told reporters.
"I endorse the intent to make our children proficient in standard American English," Jackson said, but he stopped short of endorsing the specifics of the black English plan.

The Oakland resolution, approved this month by the school board, called on the district to provide teacher and parent training in black English, or so-called Ebonics, recognise Ebonics as distinct from standard English and help black students who use Ebonics to master standard English.
Jackson said black students and others were often marginalized and needed more resources. "The challenge is to stop ignoring the youth in the margins," he said.
Jackson said he considered Ebonics a "language pattern," rather than a distinct language, adding that Oakland's intention was "not to elevate the pattern to a language."
In its resolution, the Oakland school board described black English as a distinct language, rather than a dialect of standard English.

After it was passed, Oakland's plan came under sharp attack from local officials, the state and some prominent black Americans. Initially, Jackson said the school board's decision would undermine black students' chances for success.
The Clinton administration criticised Oakland's proposal, saying it would refuse to grant special funding.
Oakland school officials insist that their critics did not understand the resolution and welcomed Jackson's supportive statement Monday.

The district said it would not teach Ebonics, derived from the words ebony and phonics, in place of standard English and would not try to classify Ebonics-speaking black students as bilingual in order to obtain federal funds.

Many Americans consider black English to be little more than inner-city slang or broken English. The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association has classified black English as a social dialect with its own lexicon and syntax.

The district contends black English is the primary language of many of its black students, who may fall behind in school because the language they use at home and on the streets may be different from the standard English used in the classroom.
By recognising Ebonics, Oakland officials said they hoped to improve the way black students are taught to read and write standard English.
An estimated 53 percent of Oakland's nearly 52,000 students are black and district officials say they have the lowest average grade point averages in the district.
